build-storybook.//: Storybook's sources are exactly the two things the `production` named input throws away — `*.stories.*` and `.storybook/**` — so the inferred `['production', '^production']` left this target with no real inputs at all, and `storybook build` served a stale build from the cache after an edit to either. The exclusions stay: they are what stops a story invalidating the app and library builds it has nothing to do with. This target opts out of them instead, by hashing `default` (the same fileset, un-subtracted) rather than `production`. Re-adding the two globs on top of `production` does NOT work and was measured, not assumed: Nx applies every `!` pattern in an input list to the whole list, so a later positive glob cannot undo an earlier exclusion — with `{projectRoot}/.storybook/**/*` restated here, editing `.storybook/main.ts` still reported `Cache: 1/1 hit`. The `{workspaceRoot}` glob is separate and not optional: `.storybook/main.ts` reaches the stories by FILE GLOB across the sibling libraries rather than by import, so Nx sees no dependency edge to them (`nx show projects --affected --files=libs/components/banner/...` does not list the host) and no amount of `^production` can reach them. It names the tier's whole `src` rather than only `*.stories.*` because a story imports the component it documents — a component edit changes this build's output just as much.

test.//: Memory is bounded by the vitest pool, not from here — see the `pool` comment in vite.base.config.ts. This used to set VITEST_MAX_THREADS=2 to cap each worker pool; that was aimed at the wrong thing (a CPU invariant for a memory-bound failure), it held while the suite still failed, and under the `forks` pool the variable is a no-op anyway since it only writes poolOptions.threads/vmThreads.

typecheck.//: The ONLY gate that type-checks specs. Every project's tsconfig.json excludes `src/**/*.spec.ts`, the type-aware ESLint block ignores them too, and Vitest goes through @analogjs/vite-plugin-angular, which transpiles without checking — so until this existed a spec could drift arbitrarily far from the code it claims to test (a fake client missing 358 MatrixClient members, a mock tuple the assertions index past the end of) and every gate stayed green. `^production` for the same reason lint needs it: a spec's types come from its DEPENDENCIES' source, so a model change in data-access must invalidate its consumers' cached pass.

lint.//: `^production` is load-bearing: @typescript-eslint/no-deprecated is type-aware, so a project's lint result depends on its DEPENDENCIES' source (the @deprecated tag lives there). Without dependency inputs, deprecating an export in util-matrix leaves every consumer reporting a cached pass — the ban silently stops working across exactly the lib boundaries it exists to police.
